usage: 안 (inner) + 방 (room); the biggest/main bedroom, usually for the couple or whoever leads the household
location marker 에 for 'where something is'
the en-suite bathroom attached to 안방, a big selling point in Korean apartments
common when roommates or family decide who gets 안방
examples: 저는 안방 쓰고, 동생은 작은방 써요.
I use the master bedroom and my younger sibling uses the small room.
작은방 (small room) is the natural pair word for 안방
안방에 화장실이 딸려 있어서 편해요.
It's convenient because the master bedroom has an attached bathroom.
딸려 있다 = 'comes attached'; very common phrase in apartment listings
집 보러 갔는데 안방이 생각보다 넓더라고요.
I went to see the place and the master bedroom was bigger than I expected.
-더라고요 reports a personal observation; natural when describing a viewing
nuance: 안방 isn't just any large room, it's culturally the 'main' bedroom of the home, traditionally where the head of the household sleeps. When flat-hunting or splitting rooms with a roommate, 안방 vs 작은방 is the standard way Koreans divide bedrooms, and 안방 usually has the en-suite bathroom.
mistakes: Calling any bedroom 안방. Only the main/largest one is 안방; the others are 작은방 or just 방.
Confusing 안방 with 거실 (living room). 안방 is a private bedroom, not the shared living area.

usage: 다용도 (multi-purpose) + 실 (room); the small back room off the kitchen for the washer, storage, and recycling
where you stash bulky items and do laundry
the washing machine is in the utility room
the washer is almost always here, not in a bathroom
it gets cluttered fast, so cleaning it is a real chore
examples: 세탁기랑 김치냉장고는 다용도실에 둬요.
I keep the washing machine and the kimchi fridge in the utility room.
김치냉장고 in the 다용도실 is extremely typical of Korean homes
다용도실에 짐을 너무 쌓아 놔서 발 디딜 데가 없어요.
I've piled up so much stuff in the utility room that there's no room to step.
발 디딜 데가 없다 = idiom for 'no space to step', very natural here
이 집은 다용도실이 따로 있어서 마음에 들어요.
I like this place because it has a separate utility room.
다용도실이 따로 있다 is a common plus point when choosing an apartment
nuance: Almost every Korean apartment (아파트) has a 다용도실, a small enclosed space off the kitchen, often behind the 베란다, where the washing machine, kimchi fridge, cleaning supplies, and recycling live. Listings proudly mention it. If you live here, you'll use this word constantly when talking about laundry or storage.
mistakes: Assuming laundry happens in the bathroom like in some Western homes. In Korea the washer is in the 다용도실 (or 베란다).
Mixing up 다용도실 (utility room) with 창고 (storage/warehouse). 다용도실 is an active work/storage space inside the home.

usage: 신발 (shoes) + 장 (cabinet); the built-in cabinet at the entrance where you store shoes
to put into the shoe cabinet
넣다 = to put in; what you do after taking your shoes off
a constant complaint, especially for people with many shoes
정리 = tidying; a frequent small chore at the 현관
examples: 신발 벗고 신발장에 넣어 주세요.
Please take off your shoes and put them in the shoe cabinet.
Said to guests; taking shoes off indoors is mandatory in Korean homes
신발장이 꽉 차서 새 운동화 둘 데가 없어요.
The shoe cabinet is full, so there's nowhere to put my new sneakers.
꽉 차다 = to be packed full; very natural daily speech
택배는 신발장 위에 올려 두시면 돼요.
You can just leave the delivery on top of the shoe cabinet.
Common instruction to a delivery driver; 위에 올려 두다 = leave on top
nuance: The 신발장 sits right at the 현관 (entryway) and is part of daily ritual: shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. Most apartments have a built-in one. It's also a handy surface, people often drop keys, masks, or deliveries on top of it.
mistakes: Calling it 신발 박스 or 신발 상자 (a shoe box). The furniture piece is 신발장.
Forgetting the shoe-removal rule. You don't just walk in, you put shoes in the 신발장 first.

usage: a single flat board mounted on a wall or inside a cabinet for putting things on
to set up on a shelf
올려 두다 = to place up (and leave); typical action with a shelf
달다 = to mount/install; what you do with a drill or adhesive
벽 (wall) + 선반; popular in small apartments to save floor space
examples: 책은 그냥 선반에 올려 두세요.
Just set the books on the shelf.
그냥 ('just') softens the instruction, very natural casual tone
화장실에 선반 하나 달았더니 훨씬 깔끔해졌어요.
After I put up one shelf in the bathroom, it got much tidier.
-았더니 shows result of an action; common when describing a small home upgrade
선반이 높아서 발판 없이는 손이 안 닿아요.
The shelf is so high I can't reach it without a step stool.
손이 안 닿다 = can't reach; everyday expression
nuance: 선반 is a single shelf board, not a whole bookcase (that's 책장). In tiny Korean officetels and one-rooms, wall-mounted 선반 are a go-to space saver, sold cheaply at 다이소 and IKEA. You'll hear it for kitchen, bathroom, and entryway storage alike.
mistakes: Using 선반 for a full bookshelf unit. A standing bookcase is 책장; 선반 is just one shelf/ledge.
Confusing 선반 (shelf) with 서랍 (drawer). A 선반 is open; a 서랍 slides out.

usage: 거실 (living room) + 장 (cabinet); the long low unit the TV sits on
on top of the TV stand
where the TV and remote usually go
a common furniture purchase when moving in
the drawer of the TV stand
거실장 often has drawers for remotes and cables
examples: 거실장 위에 티비 올려놨어요.
I put the TV on top of the living-room cabinet.
티비 (casual for TV) + 올려놓다 = to set on top; everyday phrasing
이사하면서 거실장을 새로 하나 장만했어요.
When I moved, I got myself a new TV stand.
장만하다 = to acquire/get (a bigger purchase); natural for furniture
리모컨은 거실장 서랍 안에 있을 거예요.
The remote is probably in the drawer of the TV stand.
-(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a guess; a very real daily situation
nuance: 거실장 is the low, wide cabinet that anchors a Korean living room, the TV goes on top and remotes, cables, and odds-and-ends hide in its drawers and doors. It's one of the first big furniture pieces people buy or inherit when setting up a home, so it comes up a lot in moving and shopping talk.
mistakes: Calling it 티비 책상 or 티비 테이블. The standard furniture term is 거실장 (TV 다이 is also heard informally).
Confusing 거실장 with 거실 (the living room itself). 거실장 is the furniture; 거실 is the room.

usage: 화장 (makeup) + 대 (stand/table); the table with a mirror for getting ready
where you sit to do makeup or skincare
거울 (mirror) is the defining feature of a 화장대
cosmetics pile up fast, so this is a regular chore
examples: 아침마다 화장대 앞에서 한참 앉아 있어요.
Every morning I sit in front of the vanity for ages.
한참 = for a good while; relatable morning routine talk
화장품이 많아서 화장대가 항상 지저분해요.
I have so much makeup that my vanity is always messy.
지저분하다 = messy/cluttered; natural complaint
원룸이라 화장대 놓을 자리가 없어서 그냥 거울만 붙였어요.
Since it's a one-room, there's no space for a vanity, so I just stuck a mirror up.
놓을 자리가 없다 = no space to place it; common small-apartment reality
nuance: A 화장대 is the dedicated table-with-mirror where you do makeup and skincare. In small Korean apartments it's a coveted but space-hungry item, so many renters skip it for a wall mirror. The word also signals 'getting ready' space generally, even men use 화장대 for grooming setups.
mistakes: Confusing 화장대 (vanity) with 화장실 (bathroom/toilet). They share 화장 but mean totally different things.
Using 책상 (desk) for it. A makeup table specifically is a 화장대.

usage: 옷 (clothes) + 걸이 (a thing to hang on); both the small hanger and a standing rack
걸다 = to hang; the core verb that pairs with 옷걸이
useful at a store, hotel, or asking a roommate
the freestanding pole-type rack, common in one-rooms
examples: 코트는 옷걸이에 걸어 두세요.
Please hang your coat on the hanger.
걸어 두다 = hang up (and leave); said to a guest
옷걸이가 모자라서 옷이 자꾸 쌓여요.
I don't have enough hangers, so clothes keep piling up.
모자라다 = to be short/insufficient; everyday frustration
원룸엔 붙박이장이 없어서 스탠드 옷걸이 하나 샀어요.
My one-room has no built-in closet, so I bought a standing coat rack.
links to 붙박이장; a very typical renter solution
nuance: 옷걸이 covers both the individual hanger and a standing/wall coat rack, context tells you which. In compact Korean rentals without a proper 옷장 or 붙박이장, a 스탠드 옷걸이 is the default way to hang clothes. It's an everyday word you'll use at home, in stores, and in hotels.
mistakes: Confusing 옷걸이 (hanger) with 옷장 (wardrobe). 옷걸이 is the hanging tool/rack; 옷장 is the closed cabinet.
Saying 옷 걸기 for the object. The noun is 옷걸이; 걸기 is the act of hanging.

usage: 붙박이 (fixed/built-in) + 장 (cabinet); a wardrobe built into the wall, you can't move it
a major plus when renting; saves buying an 옷장
to put into the built-in closet
where you store seasonal clothes and bedding
옵션 = built-in feature; agents list it as a selling point
examples: 이 집은 붙박이장이 있어서 옷장을 따로 안 사도 돼요.
This place has a built-in closet, so I don't need to buy a separate wardrobe.
직접적인 장점; a real reason people pick a unit
붙박이장이 커서 이불이랑 캐리어까지 다 들어가요.
The built-in closet is big, so even the bedding and suitcase fit in.
links to 이불; -까지 = even, emphasizing capacity
전에 살던 집은 붙박이장이 없어서 너무 불편했어요.
My previous place had no built-in closet, so it was really inconvenient.
전에 살던 집 = the place I used to live; natural comparison
nuance: 붙박이장 is a wall-mounted, immovable wardrobe that comes with the apartment. For renters it's hugely practical because it removes the need (and cost) of buying and moving an 옷장. Real-estate listings highlight 붙박이장 as a key 옵션, so you'll see and hear it constantly while flat-hunting.
mistakes: Treating 붙박이장 as movable furniture. By definition it's fixed to the wall; a free-standing one is just an 옷장.
Dropping a syllable and writing 붓박이장 or 붙바기장. The correct spelling is 붙박이장.

usage: the head pillow you sleep on; spelled 베개, not 배개
to rest one's head on a pillow
베다 is the dedicated verb; 베개 literally is 'the thing you 베다 on'
커버 = cover; you wash this regularly
height/firmness is the main thing people care about
examples: 베개가 너무 높아서 목이 아파요.
The pillow is too high, so my neck hurts.
목이 아프다 = neck hurts; the most common pillow complaint
새 베개로 바꿨더니 잠이 훨씬 잘 와요.
After I switched to a new pillow, I sleep much better.
잠이 잘 오다 = to fall asleep well; very natural phrasing
베개 커버는 일주일에 한 번씩 빨아요.
I wash the pillowcase once a week.
일주일에 한 번씩 = once a week each; everyday frequency expression
nuance: 베개 is the sleeping pillow, and Koreans care a lot about its height and firmness (목베개 'neck pillow', 메모리폼 'memory foam' are common follow-ups). Note the spelling trap: it's 베개 (with the verb 베다 'to lay your head on'), not the frequently-misspelled 배개. A decorative throw pillow is instead a 쿠션.
mistakes: Spelling it 배개. The correct form is 베개, from the verb 베다.
Using 베개 for a sofa throw pillow. That's a 쿠션 (cushion); 베개 is specifically for sleeping.

usage: the main bed covering you sleep under; covers comforters and floor-bedding alike
to cover oneself with a blanket
덮다 = to cover; the verb that pairs with 이불
개다 = to fold; a morning habit, especially with floor bedding
bulky laundry you take to a coin laundromat (빨래방)
examples: 밤에 추우니까 이불 잘 덮고 자.
It's cold at night, so cover yourself well with the blanket and sleep.
casual command to a friend/family; warm, caring tone
겨울 이불은 너무 두꺼워서 세탁기에 안 들어가요.
The winter duvet is so thick it won't fit in the washing machine.
links to 다용도실/빨래; a real practical problem
주말마다 이불 빨아서 햇볕에 말려요.
Every weekend I wash the bedding and dry it in the sun.
햇볕에 말리다 = to sun-dry; common Korean habit on 베란다
nuance: 이불 is the all-purpose word for the blanket/duvet/comforter you sleep under, whether on a bed or laid on the floor (이부자리). It's tied to seasonal swaps (여름 이불 vs 겨울 이불) and to the chore of bulky bedding laundry, which often means a trip to a 빨래방. A thin summer one is sometimes 홑이불.
mistakes: Confusing 이불 (blanket/duvet) with 베개 (pillow) or 침대 (bed). 이불 is the covering you sleep under.
Using 담요 for all of it. 담요 is a small lap/throw blanket; the main bed bedding is 이불.

usage: the flat cushion you sit on, on the floor or on a hard chair
깔다 = to spread/lay down; what you do before sitting on the floor
앉다 = to sit; the natural pair verb
casual phrase when hosting someone at a low table
examples: 바닥에 방석 깔고 앉으세요.
Please lay out a cushion and sit on the floor.
very common when seating a guest at a 좌식 (floor-level) table
의자가 딱딱해서 방석을 하나 올려놨어요.
The chair is hard, so I put a cushion on it.
딱딱하다 = hard; 방석 also used to soften chairs
손님 오면 방석이 모자랄 것 같아요.
When guests come I think we'll be short on cushions.
모자라다 = to run short; realistic hosting worry
nuance: 방석 is the flat sit-on cushion central to Korea's floor-sitting culture, you'll see stacks of them for guests, at floor-seating restaurants, and on hard dining chairs. It's distinct from a 쿠션 (a soft decorative/back cushion) and from 베개 (sleeping pillow). Pulling out a 방석 for a visitor is a small but real act of hospitality.
mistakes: Confusing 방석 (sit-on cushion) with 쿠션 (soft throw/back cushion) or 베개 (pillow).
Linking 방석 to 방 ('room'). Despite the spelling, 방석 means a seat cushion, not a room item.

usage: loanword from English; the padded sleeping surface on a bed frame
푹신하다 = plush; firmness is the key buying factor
renters often skip the frame and buy only this
vacuuming/airing it out is a real chore
examples: 저는 침대 프레임 없이 매트리스만 바닥에 깔고 자요.
I sleep with just a mattress on the floor, without a bed frame.
프레임 없이 = without a frame; a very common budget/one-room setup
매트리스가 너무 딱딱해서 허리가 배겨요.
The mattress is so firm my back gets sore.
배기다 = (a hard surface) digs in; natural mattress complaint
매트리스는 무거워서 혼자 옮기기 힘들어요.
The mattress is heavy, so it's hard to move alone.
옮기기 힘들다 = hard to move; relevant on moving day
nuance: 매트리스 is the everyday loanword for a mattress. In Korea many renters buy a 매트리스 alone and place it directly on the floor or on a low platform, skipping a full 침대 frame to save money and space. Firmness talk (딱딱하다 vs 푹신하다) and the hassle of moving its bulk are common conversation points.
mistakes: Equating 매트리스 with 침대. 침대 is the whole bed (frame + mattress); 매트리스 is only the sleeping pad.
Misspelling it 매트레스 or 메트리스. The standard form is 매트리스.
